(i) High cloud cover
(ii) Low dew point temperature
(iii) Low relative humidity
(iv) High relative humidity

B (ii) and (iii)

Y: pollution dome
Z: heat island

A factor contributing to higher temperatures in the urban area.
Y: dense buildings
Z: green belts

Heat islands are more dominant during the …
Y: day
Z: night

Y: Planting trees
Z: Tarring roads

Multiple reflections of the sun's rays in urban areas are caused by …

Z: concrete surfaces

Heat islands are more likely to favour the formation of …
Y: smog

… is an effect of heat islands on people.

Z: Reduced visibility
The general direction of movement of the cold front is (eastwards/westwards).
Why does the mid-latitude cyclone move in this direction (answer to QUESTION 1.3.1)?
subQuestions.memoText: The mid-latitude cyclone is steered by the westerlies. / This cyclone occurs in the westerly wind belt. [ANY ONE] (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Account for the heavy rainfall of 80% at A as the cold front approaches.
subQuestions.memoText: The cold air undercuts the warm air (2); The warm air is rapidly uplifted along the cold front (2); Results in rapid cooling of air (2); (Vertical) condensation takes place (2); Formation of cumulonimbus clouds (2). [ANY TWO] (2 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, explain how different weather conditions associated with a cold front will have a negative impact on tourists in the Western Cape.
subQuestions.memoText: Weather conditions must be linked to a negative impact. Weather conditions include: heavy rainfall/thunderstorms, strong/gusty winds, snow, low temperatures, lightning, overcast conditions, frontal fog/mist, hail. Impacts include: outdoor activities being cancelled (2); tourist destinations inaccessible (2); marine craft unable to go out to sea (2); flooding of tourist attractions/coastal areas (2); suspended flights causing financial losses (2); transport routes dangerous (2); outdoor activities dangerous for tourists (2); tourists get sick (2); poor visibility increases accidents (2); mass movements dangerous for tourists (2); power outages affecting accommodation (2). [ANY FOUR weather condition + impact pairs] (4 x 2). If only qualifiers mentioned, no marks awarded.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE piece of evidence from the satellite image which shows that the tropical cyclone is in the Southern Hemisphere.
subQuestions.memoText: Clockwise circulation of air around the eye. (1 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Name the area of the cyclone labelled A.
Why does air subside in area A?
subQuestions.memoText: (Upper air) Convergence/accumulation of air above the eye (2) / A pressure gradient is created (higher pressure above the eye) (2) / Air above the eye is cold and dense (2). [ANY ONE] (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Draw the symbol that is used on a synoptic weather map to represent a tropical cyclone in the Southern Hemisphere.
subQuestions.memoText: A clockwise rotating spiral symbol (rotation must be clockwise). (1 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the formation of high-density clouds at B.
subQuestions.memoText: Rapid evaporation/upliftment of warm air over warm oceans (2); Intense updrafts/convection currents/strong pressure gradient occurs at B (2); Rapid cooling of air (2); This will favour rapid (vertical) condensation (2). [ANY TWO] (2 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: High-density clouds result in torrential (very heavy) rainfall. Describe the natural (physical) environmental damage associated with this torrential rainfall as it moves over the land.
subQuestions.memoText: Coastal erosion would take place (2); soil erosion would occur on the land (2); mass movements change the landscape (2); reshaping of the coastline (2); habitats would be destroyed (2); food chains/food webs are destroyed (2); biodiversity would be diminished (2); contamination of water sources (2); silting up of rivers (2); increased leaching of nutrients (2). [ANY THREE] (3 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: What are berg winds?
subQuestions.memoText: Hot dry winds that blow from the interior (down the escarpment) to the coast. [CONCEPT] (1 x 2). Accept part marks: Hot, dry winds (1); Blows from the interior (down the escarpment) to the coast (1).

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO factors evident on the map that promote berg wind conditions.
subQuestions.memoText: (Kalahari) High-pressure cell (1); Coastal low-pressure cell (1). (2 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: According to the extract, why does the temperature of the air increase as it blows from Johannesburg to Durban?
subQuestions.memoText: It undergoes heating caused by the adiabatic process (1) / It heats up by approximately 1°C per 100 metres as it descends (1). [ANY ONE] (1 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the expected air temperature at Durban due to the associated berg wind conditions.
Why is the threat of wildfires greater during the day when berg winds occur?
subQuestions.memoText: Higher air temperatures (2); Greater amount of evaporation/dries out vegetation (2); Low relative humidity (dry air) increases the possibility of fires (2); More human activities occur that can start a fire (2). [ANY TWO] (2 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why berg winds are associated with lower agricultural productivity on farms.
subQuestions.memoText: Dry (windy) conditions damage crops/pastural land (2); dry (windy) conditions cause soil erosion (2); high temperatures cause livestock/crops to wither/die (2); strong winds fan fires that destroy farmland/infrastructure (2); wildfires associated with berg winds kill livestock/damage crops (2); high temperatures cause heat stress which reduces workers' productivity (2); increased evaporation reduces soil moisture content (2). [ANY TWO] (2 x 2). If only qualifiers mentioned, no marks awarded.

C inclined strata.
D major faults.

In drainage pattern Q, the stream order at X is … and could … with heavy rainfall.

The sketch that depicts turbulent flow.
Y: [sketch of laminar/straight flow]
Z: [sketch of turbulent/wavy flow]

The fluvial process associated with turbulent flow.
Y: deposition
Z: erosion

The fluvial feature associated with turbulent flow.
Y: rapid
Z: levee

The sketch that depicts a cross-profile.
Y: [sketch showing cross-profile]
Z: [sketch showing long profile]

An example of an ungraded river profile.
Y: [sketch of smooth graded profile]
Z: [sketch of ungraded/stepped profile]

… of rivers can change the grade of a river from graded to ungraded.
Y: Rejuvenation
Z: Meandering

A waterfall is an example of a … base level of erosion.
Y: permanent
Z: temporary
Braided streams and deltas form when the dominant fluvial process is (erosion/deposition).
State ONE physical similarity between braided streams and deltas.
subQuestions.memoText: Both branch off into smaller channels (2) / Both have sand islands (2) / Velocity of the river is low (2) / Shallow stream channel (2) / Both have a wide river channel (2) / Both rivers experience laminar flow (2). [ANY ONE] (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Give TWO reasons why braided streams are common in the lower course of a river.
subQuestions.memoText: The gradient is gentle (2); speed of the river decreases (2); lower carrying capacity of the water (2); (increased) deposition/bedload (2); laminar flow dominates (2); wider stream channel (2); shallow stream channels (2). [ANY TWO] (2 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Why do deltas not form in all rivers?
subQuestions.memoText: Less silt/sediment deposited (2); strong ocean currents/tidal action (2); some rivers have a steep gradient at the mouth (2); deep continental shelf (2). [ANY TWO] (2 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why deltas are suitable for agriculture.
subQuestions.memoText: They provide fertile soil for crop farming (2); flat land allows for use of machinery (2); access to water supply from the distributaries for irrigation (2); distributaries create transport routes for farming products (2). [ANY TWO] (2 x 2). If only qualifiers mentioned, no marks awarded.

subQuestions.questionText: What is headward erosion?
subQuestions.memoText: River cutting/eroding backwards through the watershed (2) / Erosion towards the source (2) / River lengthening from the source (2). [CONCEPT - ANY ONE] (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: State ONE factor evident on the sketch that would promote headward erosion in stream A.
subQuestions.memoText: The steeper gradient (1) / Flowing at a lower level (1). [ANY ONE] (1 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is stream A referred to as the captor stream after river capture?
subQuestions.memoText: It has captured the headwaters of stream B. (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is river gravel found in the wind gap after river capture?
subQuestions.memoText: After the elbow of capture there is less water flowing/reduced carrying capacity (2); sediment is deposited (2). (2 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how the fluvial processes would change in stream A after river capture.
subQuestions.memoText: Erosion will increase (2); vertical erosion will increase (2); lateral erosion will increase (2); transportation will increase (2); deposition will decrease (2). [ANY THREE] (3 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: According to the extract, state TWO ways in which mines pollute rivers.
subQuestions.memoText: Mining chemicals (1); mining waste (1); mine dumps (1); surface runoff (1); seepage from mine dumps (1). [ANY TWO] (2 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Quote from the extract ONE health risk that mining poses for humans.
Explain the negative impact of mining on the river system.
subQuestions.memoText: It (river system) could become polluted (2); the pH level could change/acid/poisonous (2); eutrophication occurs/more algae in the water (2); water quality will decrease (2); reduces river's carrying capacity (2); biodiversity is diminished (2); food chains/food webs are destroyed (2); habitats are destroyed (2). [ANY TWO] (2 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, suggest measures that mining companies can implement to manage the impact of water pollution on rivers and humans.
subQuestions.memoText: Employ environmental officers (2); improved waste management (2); maintain/improve mining infrastructure (2); implement monitoring/testing (2); develop treatment technologies (2); neutralise the acidic water (2); use of biodegradable (less harmful) chemicals (2); rehabilitate mine dumps (2); buffer areas to protect rivers (2); access to medical assistance (2); educate workers/community (2); awareness campaigns (2); build slimes dam to pump water in (2). [ANY FOUR] (4 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the length of the Wagendrift Dam wall at F in block C3 in metres (m).

Formula: Actual distance = Map distance x Map scale
subQuestions.memoText: Map distance: 0,6 cm (accept range 0,5–0,7 cm) (1); Actual distance = 0,6 x 50 000 = 30 000 cm = 300 m (accept range 250 m–350 m) (1). (2 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the magnetic declination for 2025 using the following information:
Difference in years: 24 years
Mean annual change: 9' W
Draw a rough cross-section from 6 in block A4 to 7 in block B5.
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark for convex slope (from point 6 side); 1 mark for concave slope (toward point 7 side). (2 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is there no intervisibility between 6 and 7?
subQuestions.memoText: There is a convex slope (1). (Accept: there is an obstruction/crest.) [ANY ONE] (1 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Name the wind that is likely to blow at night between G and H.
Give ONE reason why this wind (answer to QUESTION 3.2.1) will develop in this area.

subQuestions.label: 3.2.3(a)
subQuestions.questionText: The rate of evaporation will be less in area (8/9).

subQuestions.label: 3.2.3(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Give evidence from the orthophoto map for the low rate of evaporation in this area (answer to QUESTION 3.2.3(a)).
subQuestions.memoText: It is a built-up area (2) / It is made up of artificial surfaces/less vegetation (2) / Drainage (infrastructure) channels water away (2). [ANY ONE] (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE strategy that was put in place to limit the negative human impact on the Wagendrift Dam.
subQuestions.memoText: It was declared a nature reserve (2) / It was declared a protected area/buffering of area (2). [ANY ONE] (1 x 2)

subQuestions.label: 3.2.5(a)
subQuestions.questionText: Identify fluvial landform/feature 10 on the orthophoto map.

subQuestions.label: 3.2.5(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Feature 11 is known as the (inner/outer) bank.

subQuestions.label: 3.2.5(c)
subQuestions.questionText: Why will this bank (answer to QUESTION 3.2.5(b)) be associated with fertile soil?
subQuestions.memoText: Deposition takes place (on the inner bank/point bar). (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: What is data layering?
subQuestions.memoText: Different data layers of information (with specific themes) placed on top of one another. [CONCEPT] (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify TWO infrastructural layers in block B1 that would promote farming.
subQuestions.memoText: Transport/Roads/Bridge (1); Buildings (1); Dam wall (accept perennial water/dam) (1); Communication Tower (1). [ANY TWO] (2 x 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Define the concept remote sensing.
subQuestions.memoText: Collection of information of the earth from a (vertical) distance (without any contact with the earth). [CONCEPT] (1 x 2)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to blocks C1/C2 and D1/D2. How would remote sensing assist the town's emergency personnel in the event of flooding of the Bushmans River?
subQuestions.memoText: Able to source information from inaccessible areas (2); rescue efforts will be prompt (2); emergency personnel would be able to take less risks (2); continual monitoring would lead to effective action (2); information will be updated regularly (2); identify areas at high risk of flooding (2); put in place early warning system (2). [ANY ONE] (1 x 2)
